title: The Worst Line in Verrin
part: PART ONE: THE SHOP AT THE END OF INK LANE

pages.text:
*The Third Rule of Mapmaking: Compare your line only with yesterday's.*

The afternoon light fell in slanting bars across the drawing table, catching dust motes that drifted with an annoying precision. Tam sat before a lumpy piece of driftwood, which Finch had placed there to represent the coastline of the island of Crag.

"Draw what you see," Finch said from her chair, watching with a stillness that felt like being measured.

Tam uncapped her ink pot. She dipped the nib and hesitated. The paper seemed to hold its breath. She made the first stroke. It was shaky. The second stroke was worse. Then, as if the ink had decided to rebel, the nib caught a fiber in the paper. The pen jumped. A splatter of black hit the middle of the sea, expanding into a dark, wet circle the size of a plum.

Tam stared at it. The blot gazed back.

She tore the sheet off, picked up a new one, and drew again. The line wavered like a reed in a gale. The blot returned, larger this time. She tore it up, then kicked the wooden stool, sending it skidding across the floorboards with a loud, accusing scrape.

"Steady," Finch said, not looking up from her book.

"It is not steady," Tam muttered, her cheeks burning. "The ink is steady. The island is not."
pages.image: Tam, a sturdy 11-year-old girl with a black braid and blue string, sits at a cluttered desk, staring angrily at a large black ink blot on paper; a small wooden island model sits nearby, and a stool lies tipped over on the floor.

pages.text:
A knock at the door interrupted the silence. Finch nodded toward it. Tam opened the door to find a young servant in a green livery, holding a sealed envelope with the wax crest of House Ravel. He handed it over with a polite bow and scurried away, his shoes clicking rapidly on the cobbles.

Finch broke the seal. Inside was a sheet of heavy, cream-colored paper. It was Lucan Ravel’s sample map, sent as a courtesy to the participating masters.

The coast was perfect. It was not just accurate; it was elegant. The lines flowed with a confidence that made Tam’s own scribbles look like the work of a blind mouse. In the corner, a tiny sea serpent curled around the compass rose, its scales rendered in minute, precise dots.

Tam picked up her own sheet. The plum-sized blot stared up at her. She looked at Lucan’s serpent. She looked at her blot. The air in the shop seemed to drain away, leaving a hollow, ringing quiet.

"I'll never draw like that," she whispered.

The whisper was so soft that Finch, who had been turning her spectacles in her hands, stopped and looked at her. The fear in Tam’s voice was colder and sharper than any shout could have been.
pages.image: Tam holds a sheet of paper with a large ink blot, staring at it with downcast eyes; beside her on the table lies a pristine, elegant map with intricate details, contrasting sharply with her messy work.

pages.text:
Finch did not offer comfort. She did not offer a lecture. She stood, tapped her cane once on the floor, and climbed the crooked stairs. The steps groaned. A familiar complaint.

When she returned, a rolled bundle sat under her arm. It was tied with a fraying ribbon. She unrolled it on the table.

The map was yellowed. Brittle at the edges. Mice had chewed two distinct holes in the corner. The coastline was a tangle of wobbly brown lines. It looked less like a shore and more like a spilled plate of noodles. The compass rose leaned to the left. It looked tired. In the middle of the land, a single crude tree stood. Next to it, in shaky letters, was the label: "Big Tree (?)."

Tam stared. A giggle bubbled up in her throat. Unwanted. Sudden. She clamped her hand over her mouth. It slipped out anyway. A dry, startled sound. Then she laughed harder, until she sat on the edge of the bench to keep from falling over.

"Sixty years ago," Finch said. A genuine smile broke across her lined face. "Look how far a person can travel."
pages.image: Master Finch, a tall thin woman in a lavender scarf, smiles warmly while holding out a crumpled, yellowed map with a crude drawing of a tree and wobbly lines; Tam sits on a bench, hand over her mouth, laughing with delight.

pages.text:
"The trouble with looking at Lucan’s map," Finch said, her voice low and steady, "is that you are comparing your beginning to his middle." She tapped the mouse-nibbled parchment, then moved it aside to make room for the small, stitched notebook. "You will always find someone who is better, and you will also always find someone who is worse. Neither one helps you draw the next line."

"Open it," she said, pointing with her hawthorn cane.

Tam flipped through the pages. At first, the rivers looked identical, just a series of crooked, wobbly, imperfect brown lines. But as her eyes moved from page to page, a pattern emerged. The first river was jagged. The second was slightly smoother. The third had a bend that was just a fraction more controlled, like a child learning to write their name without shaking.

"It is a staircase," Finch said. "A slow, stubborn staircase going upward. You do not need to reach the top today. You only need to step one rung higher than yesterday."

Tam looked at the lines again. She did not see a failure. She saw a path. Each line was a proof that she had tried, and that the trying had changed the shape of the ink.
pages.image: Tam’s hands hold open a small notebook filled with hand-drawn, wavy lines that gradually become smoother; Master Finch’s trembling finger points to the progression, highlighting the subtle improvement in the drawings.

pages.text:
That evening, the shop was quiet. Candles burned low, casting long shadows against the walls. Tam sat at her table, uncapped her ink, and picked up her pen.

She drew the river. The two-bend river. The same one she had drawn every night for seven months.

Her hand moved slowly. She did not look at the wall. She did not think of Lucan’s serpent. She thought only of the line before her, and the line she had drawn yesterday.

When she finished, she held the new sheet up. She placed it beside the previous night’s drawing.

The new line was a hair straighter. The bend was a little more deliberate. The blot at the corner was there, but it was smaller, less aggressive.

Tam picked up her fine-point pen. She wrote beneath the drawing, in small, careful letters: *Straighter by a whisker. Blot at the corner, but smaller.*

She looked at it for a long time. The shop was still. The candles flickered. It was the first time she had ever been proud of a line that was still crooked.
pages.image: Tam sits at a dimly lit table, holding up two sheets of paper side-by-side to compare two hand-drawn river lines; she looks at them with focused, quiet satisfaction, her ink-stained fingers visible against the paper.
